sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Bragi** ​(*bragi*) — ‌Poetry, Eloquence ‌· ​Poet, first ​— belongs ​to ​the Norse ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Poetry, ​Eloquence". ‌The name ​means "Poet, ‌first"[^1].

​Bragi is ​the god ​the ​North made ​out of ‌its ​own craft: ‌the god ​of ‌poetry and ​of the ‌well-turned ​word, husband ‌of Iðunn, ​the ​voice Snorri ‌seats at ‌the centre ‌of ​every divine ​feast — ‌the ​skald who ​narrates the ‌myths ​to Ægir ​in the ‌Prose ​Edda's own ‌frame, and ​the ​god Óðinn ​sends out ​to ‌greet dead ‌kings at ​the ‌door of ​Valhǫll.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ‌as **Bragi** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/bragi/). ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *bragi* ‌survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Lokasenna 11–18 (Bragi bars Loki from the feast; Iðunn's intervention); Grímnismál 44 (Bragi best of skalds, in the litany of the best).

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 26 (the catalogue portrait: eloquence, bragr from his name, husband of Iðunn); Skáldskaparmál (the frame with Ægir; the mead of poetry; the abduction of Iðunn; kennings for Bragi; quotations of Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrápa).

Eyvindr Finnsson skáldaspillir, Hákonarmál (Bragi and Hermóðr sent to greet King Hákon), preserved in Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Hákonar saga góða; and the anonymous Eiríksmál (Bragi questions Óðinn on Eiríkr Bloodaxe), preserved in Fagrskinna.

sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in Younger ​Futhark ​as ​**ᛒᚱᛅᚴᛁ**. ​Etymologically ‌it ​means ​"Poet, ‌first"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*bragi* ‌survives ​only ​because ​the ​early ​domain-name ‌system could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not an ​ancient ‌spelling. ‌The ‌Unicode ​restoration ​**Bragi** ‌recovers ​the ​full diacritic ‌detail ​of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ​in ​the address ​bar. ​The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ​a ​description ‌computed from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form ​itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**b** → ​**B** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**r** ​→ ​**r** ‌— ​Same
- **a** ‌→ ​**a** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**g** ‌→ ​**g** ​— ​Same
- **i** ​→ ‌**i** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/ˈbrɑ.ɣi/** — ​Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​For the modern ​speaker, the ​closest approximation is: ​BRAH-ghi — ‌a short open ​'ah', and ​the g softening ‌between vowels to ​a light ‌voiced fricative, like ​a gentle ‌'gh'; stress falls ​on the ​first syllable.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the ​name:

- **Old Norse** ‌— Bragi; ​genitive Braga
- **Old ‌Norse common ​noun** — bragr ‌— 'poetry', and ​'foremost, the ‌best'
- **Modern Icelandic** ​— Bragi, ‌the name's unbroken ​living form ​as a male ‌given name
- **Norwegian** ‌— Brage ‌— as in ​the Brage ​Prize, Norway's literary ‌award
- **Old ​Norse compound** — ​bragarfull — 'the ‌foremost cup', ​the vow-toast that ​kept his ‌name at the ​feast after ‌the god's cult ​faded

Old ​Norse Bragi is ​bound to the ​poetic noun ‌bragr, which carries ‌two senses ​at once: 'poetry' ‌and 'foremost, ​chief, the best' ​(Cleasby–Vigfusson, s.v. bragr). ‌Snorri derives ‌the noun from ‌the god ‌— from Bragi's ​name bragr ‌is called, and ​from it a ​man or ​woman of eloquence ‌is a ​bragr-maðr or bragr-kona ​— while ​modern etymologists argue ‌over which direction ​the derivation ​truly runs. The ​normalized Old ‌Norse form is ​plain ASCII: ‌no diacritic, no ​thorn or eth, ‌nothing for ​the ASCII alphabet ‌to lose. ‌plain-form by the ​mechanical rule ​— a statement ​about orthography, never ​about the ‌god Grímnismál calls ‌the best ​of skalds.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger ​Futhark as ​**ᛒᚱᛅᚴᛁ**.[^1]

The ​scholarly ​transliteration is ​*braki*.

The ‌rendering ​proceeds step ​by step:

- ‌ᛒ ​(bjarkan) writes ‌both /b/ ​and ‌/p/
- ᚱ ​(reið) writes ​/r/
- ​ᛅ (ár) ​writes /a/, ​/á/ ‌and /æ/
- ​The spelling ‌braki ​is a ‌normalized phonetic ​reconstruction; ‌Younger Futhark ​does not ‌distinguish ​voiced/voiceless stops ​or separate ‌short ‌and long ‌vowels

The ​normalized ​Old Norse ‌form is ​**Bragi** ​— already ‌plain ASCII, ​with ​no diacritic ‌or distinctive ​letter for ‌the ​restoration to ​recover; in ​the ​Younger Futhark ‌the name ‌would ​have been ‌carved ᛒᚱᛅᚴᛁ ​(b-r-a-k-i, ​the ᚴ ‌rune writing ‌g ‌as well ‌as k). ​Because ‌the name ​is pure ​ASCII, ​its domain ‌was registered ​decades ​ago in ​the ordinary ‌way: ​**bragi.com is ​held by ​a ‌third party ​outside the ‌PuniCodex ​collection and ‌is watched ​for ‌release** — ‌no form ​of ​the name ​is currently ​owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Bragi ​is the ‌god the ‌North made ​out of ​its own ​craft: the ​god of ​poetry and ‌of the ​well-turned word, ​husband of ‌Iðunn, the ​voice Snorri ‌seats at ​the centre ‌of every ​divine feast ​— the ​skald who ​narrates the ​myths to ‌Ægir in ​the Prose ‌Edda's own ​frame, and ‌the god ​Óðinn sends ‌out to ​greet dead ‌kings at ​the door ​of Valhǫll.[^1]

### ‌The Mead ‌of Poetry

‌The blood-and-honey ​mead brewed ​from wise ‌Kvasir, hoarded ​by Suttungr ​and stolen ‌by Óðinn ​— the ​myth of ‌poetry's origin ​that Bragi ‌himself narrates ​in Skáldskaparmál.

### ​The Bragarfull

​The 'foremost ​cup' drained ‌with binding ‌vows at ​the great ‌feasts — ​the toast ​that kept ‌the god's ‌word for ‌'foremost' at ‌the drinking-table ​long after ‌conversion.

### The ​Long Beard

​Skegg-Bragi: Skáldskaparmál's ​kenning calls ‌him the ​long-bearded god ​— the ​beard as ‌the old ​skald's visible ​mark of ​office.

### The ‌King's Welcome

​The voice ‌at Valhǫll's ​door: in ‌Hákonarmál Óðinn ​sends Bragi ‌and Hermóðr ‌out to ​greet the ​dead king ​Hákon the ​Good as ‌he comes ‌to the ​hall.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 26 (the catalogue portrait: eloquence, bragr from his name, husband of Iðunn); Skáldskaparmál (the frame with Ægir; the mead of poetry; the abduction of Iðunn; kennings for Bragi; quotations of Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrápa).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Bragi ​concentrates in ​a ​small ​set of ​recurring ‌attributes, ​each a ​compressed ‌statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ‌mead of ​poetry** ​— Poetry ​as ​a ​liquid that ‌can ​be ‌brewed, stolen, ​and ‌shared ​— inspiration ‌made ​drinkable
- ‌**The bragarfull** ​— ​The ‌foremost cup ‌of ‌the vow-toast ​— ​the ‌spoken word ​made ​binding ‌over drink
- ​**The ​long ‌beard** — ​Snorri's ‌kenning ​for the ​god ​— ​age, memory, ‌and ‌the ​skald's authority ‌worn ​on the ​face
- ‌**The ‌bench in ‌Ægir's ‌hall** ​— The ‌storyteller's ​seat ​at the ​feast ‌— ​eloquence as ​a ​hospitality ‌the gods ​themselves ​require
- **The ​greeting ‌of ​dead kings** ‌— ​The ‌word that ​meets ‌greatness ‌at death's ​door ​— ​praise as ​the ‌North's ‌answer to ​mortality

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Bragi acts in almost nothing ​and speaks in everything. His dossier is a voice: the ‌catalogue portrait in Gylfaginning, the storytelling frame of Skáldskaparmál, the ‌first sharp answer to Loki in Lokasenna, and the welcome ​spoken over dead kings in the court poems. The tradition ​made the god of poetry out of the thing poetry ​does.[^1]

### The Best of Skalds (Gylfaginning 26)

Snorri's catalogue ​of the Æsir fixes the portrait the whole tradition repeats: ​one of the gods is called Bragi; he is renowned ‌for wisdom and most of all for eloquence and skill ​with words, and he knows more about poetry than any ​other. From his name, Snorri says, bragr is called — ‌the word means both poetry and the foremost of ​anything — and from it a man or woman who ‌surpasses others in eloquence is called a bragr-maðr or bragr-kona. ​His wife is Iðunn. Grímnismál's litany of the world's best ‌things seals the verdict in verse: Bragi is best of ​skalds, as Sleipnir is best of horses and Bifrǫst of ​bridges (st. 44). A god whose office is praising ​others better than anyone is the North's most honest theology ​of art: the maker vanishes into the making.[^2]

### The Gods' ​Own Storyteller (Skáldskaparmál)

The Prose Edda's second half is built ‌around Bragi's voice. When Ægir, the sea-god skilled in magic, ​came to a feast in Ásgarðr, he was seated ‌beside Bragi, and they drank and talked — and the ​myths Bragi tells him are the ones the book exists ‌to record: how the Æsir and Vanir spat their truce ​into a vat and made Kvasir, wisest of beings; how ‌the dwarfs Fjalarr and Galarr killed him and brewed his ​blood with honey into the mead that makes a ‌skald of whoever drinks; how the mead passed to the ​giant Suttungr and how Óðinn, as Bǫlverkr, lay three nights ​with Gunnlǫð and drained Óðrerir in three gulps. Bragi also ‌tells Ægir how the giant Þjazi took the shape of ‌an eagle and carried off his own wife Iðunn and ‌her apples of youth, and how Loki won her ​back. When Skáldskaparmál later asks how Bragi himself shall be ​kennt, the answer is the god's whole identity in one ‌line: husband of Iðunn, first maker of poetry, the long-bearded ​god, and son of Óðinn.

### The First Answer in Ægir's ​Hall (Lokasenna 11–18)

When Loki forced his way into Ægir's ‌feast uninvited and demanded a place at the drinking, ​Bragi was the first of the Æsir to refuse him: ​the gods, he said, know whom they will have at ‌their high feast, and Loki is not one. Loki invoked ​Óðinn's old oath of blood-brotherhood and won his seat — ‌and then began the flyting the poem is named for. ​To Bragi he threw the insult that stings a ​skald most: that the god of the word was the ​most cowardly of the Æsir in war, shyest of the ​bow-shot when fighting came. Bragi answered that if they stood ‌outside the hall he would carry Loki's head in his ‌hand — and then it was Iðunn, his wife, who ​did the true eloquent work of the scene, begging ‌Bragi not to bandy words with Loki in Ægir's hall ​and calming the quarrel before it ran further. The poem ​keeps Bragi exactly where the tradition always keeps him: at ‌the bench, in the war of words.

### The Greeter of ‌Dead Kings (Hákonarmál · Eiríksmál)

The court poets gave Bragi ‌his most solemn office. In Eyvindr skáldaspillir's Hákonarmál, composed ‌for the funeral of King Hákon the Good around 961, ​Óðinn looks out as the slain king approaches Valhǫll with ‌his host and speaks the order the North remembered: 'Hermóðr ​and Bragi, go to meet the king — a king ​who seems mighty is coming to the hall.' In the ​anonymous Eiríksmál, woven for Eiríkr Bloodaxe, it is Bragi ‌who speaks with Óðinn inside the hall: he asks why ​the Allfather robbed Eiríkr of victory when the king seemed ​to him the bravest, and Óðinn answers with the sentence ​that explains all such losses — the grey wolf gapes ‌ever at the dwellings of the gods. The god ​of poetry is the one who must ask why the ​brave die, and the one sent out to welcome them ​home.

### Bragi Boddason and the God-Making Poet (Skáldskaparmál · Skáldatal)

‌History keeps a second Bragi, and the two have never ​been fully separated. Bragi Boddason the Old, a Norwegian skald ‌of the ninth century, is the earliest skald whose ​name and verse both survive: his Ragnarsdrápa, a shield-poem of ‌painted myths, is quoted stanza by stanza in Skáldskaparmál, and ​Skáldatal counts him among the skalds of Ragnarr loðbrók. Since ‌the nineteenth century scholars have asked whether the god is ‌the deified poet — a great court skald promoted after ​death into the pantheon he served — and the ​handbooks register the theory without settling it. Simek notes the ​other, colder possibility: that the divine Bragi may be a ​late literary personification of bragr, poetry itself, with no old ‌cult behind him at all. Between the poet made god ‌and the god made out of a noun, the sources ​leave the question honestly open.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 26 (the catalogue portrait: eloquence, bragr from his name, husband of Iðunn); Skáldskaparmál (the frame with Ægir; the mead of poetry; the abduction of Iðunn; kennings for Bragi; quotations of Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrápa).

Eyvindr Finnsson skáldaspillir, Hákonarmál (Bragi and Hermóðr sent to greet King Hákon), preserved in Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Hákonar saga góða; and the anonymous Eiríksmál (Bragi questions Óðinn on Eiríkr Bloodaxe), preserved in Fagrskinna.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Bragi invites ​comparisons, and ‌the honest ‌ones are ​typological, not ​genealogical. The ​Irish Ogma of ​the Tuatha ​Dé Danann ‌— champion ​of eloquence, ​credited with the ‌Ogham script ​— is ‌his closest ​structural kin ‌in the ​neighbouring tradition: two ​Indo-European cultures ​that each ​enthroned the ​well-spoken word ‌among their gods, ​with no ‌borrowing argued ​or needed. ‌The Greek ​comparison is ‌weaker: Bragi is ​no Apollo, ‌for he ​neither leads ​a choir ‌nor prophesies, and ‌the North ‌already gave ​the mead ​of poetry's ‌conquest to ​Óðinn. What Bragi ​has that ‌the Greeks ​never made ​into a ‌god is the ​skald's office ‌itself — ​praise as ​a profession, ​memory as ​a wage, the ‌poem as ‌the contract ​between a ‌king and ​his fame. The ​deepest syncretic ‌question is ‌internal: whether ‌Bragi is ‌a personification ​of bragr raised ‌to godhood, ​or the ​euhemerized Bragi ​Boddason absorbed ‌into his own ​subject matter. ​Either way, ​he is ‌the most ​Germanic of ​answers to the ​question of ‌where poetry ​lives: it ‌lives at ​the feast, with ‌a name ​that means ‌'foremost'.[^1]

Within ‌the Norse ​tradition, closely ​related names in ​the corpus ​include [[alfheimr|Álfheimr]], ‌[[andvari|Andvari]], [[angrboda|Angrboða]], ‌[[audhumla|Auðhumla]], [[baldr|Baldr]], ​and [[baugi|Baugi]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Bragi ​never left ‌the North's ‌language. Bragr ​remained ​the Old ​Norse word ​for ​poetry itself; ‌the bragr-maðr ​and bragr-kona ​— ‌the man ​or woman ‌of ​surpassing eloquence ‌— kept ​his name ​in ​everyday compliment; ​and the ​bragarfull, ‌the foremost ​cup of ‌the vow-toast ​that ‌Ynglinga saga ​sets at ‌the ​great inheritance ‌feasts, carried ​the word ​into ‌the drinking ‌customs of ‌medieval ​Scandinavia and, ​revived, into ‌the sumbel ​of ​modern Heathen ‌practice, where ​Bragi ​is still ‌hailed as ​the patron ‌of ​poets before ​the boasting ​rounds ​begin. The ‌name lives ‌on as ​a ‌Scandinavian given ​name — ​Bragi ‌in Iceland, ‌Brage in ‌Norway and ‌Sweden ​— and ‌Norway's premier ​literary ​award, the ​Brage Prize, ‌has borne ​it ​since 1992. The ​white-bearded Bragi ‌with ​a harp ​who appears ​in nineteenth-century ‌Scandinavian ​painting and ‌sculpture is ​a ‌Romantic addition: ​the Eddas ‌give him ‌no ​instrument, only ​the voice ​— ​which was, ‌of course, ‌the whole ​point.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Bragi ​is a ‌textual god: ‌no runestone ​invokes him, ​no votive ​deposit names ​him, and ​the place-name ‌record ​offers no ​secure theophoric ‌site — ​the silence ‌that leads ​Simek and ‌Lindow to ​weigh him ​as ​a late ​literary personification ​rather than ‌an old ​cult figure. ‌The runic ​corpus does ‌know ​the name, ‌but only ​as an ‌ordinary human ​anthroponym: Bragi ​is well ‌attested as ‌a Viking-Age ‌man's ​name in ​Scandinavian inscriptions, ‌which is ​precisely the ​problem for ‌cult-hunters, since ​none of ​the carvings ‌can ​be tied ‌to the ​god. The ​witnesses are ​therefore the ​manuscripts. Lokasenna ‌and Grímnismál ‌survive in ​the ‌thirteenth-century Codex ​Regius of ​the Poetic ‌Edda; Gylfaginning ‌and the ‌Skáldskaparmál frame ‌in the ​Codex Regius ‌and ​sister manuscripts ​of the ​Prose Edda, ‌with Skáldatal ​in the ​Uppsala codex; ​Hákonarmál rides ‌inside ​the Heimskringla ​tradition and ​Eiríksmál inside ‌Fagrskinna. The ​famous image ‌of Bragi ​as an ‌old harper ​belongs ‌to nineteenth-century ‌art, not ​to the ​material record: ​no medieval ​carving, pendant, ‌or picture ‌stone shows ​him.[^1]

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic Edda preserves Bragi in Old Norse alliterative verse. Poems such as Völuspá, Hávamál, and Grímnismál place Bragi within the cosmological drama of poetry.

The meter encodes stress and alliteration that the normalized spelling Bragi attempts to carry forward into the digital record.[^1]

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda systematizes the myths of Bragi for a thirteenth-century Icelandic audience. Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál preserve genealogies, kennings, and narratives.

These sources frame Bragi as poetry. The restoration Bragi keeps the Old Norse vowel length visible in the address bar.[^1]

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
Direct runic attestations of Bragi are not known in the surviving corpus; the name appears in medieval manuscripts rather than on rune stones. When reconstructed in Younger Futhark, the form underscores the distance between manuscript normalization and epigraphic habit.

PuniCodex displays the reconstructed runic form as the original script while noting the evidentiary gap honestly.[^1]

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Saga literature — family sagas, legendary sagas, and kings' sagas — keeps Bragi alive in prose narrative. The figure functions as poetry in stories that blend history, genealogy, and myth.

The normalized name Bragi marks the scholarly form behind these later retellings.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Bragi ​is the ‌god a ‌culture of ​oral ​memory had ​to invent. ​In ​a world ‌without archives, ​the skald ​was ‌the archive: ​the king's ‌deeds, ​the clan's ‌honour, the ​boundary between ​being ​remembered and ​being nothing ​all ‌ran through ​one trained ‌voice at ​the ‌feast. The ​North looked ‌at ​that voice ‌and saw ​a god ​in ‌it — ‌and then, ‌characteristically, ​put the ​god to ‌work at ​the ​door of ‌the dead, ​because ​the only ‌immortality the ​Edda truly ‌promises ​is the ​welcome spoken ​over ​you when ‌you arrive. ‌Óðinn wins ​the ‌mead; Bragi ​pours it. ​That ‌division of ‌labour is ‌the deepest ‌thing ​the tradition ‌says about ​poetry: ​inspiration is ​theft and ‌ordeal, but ​eloquence ​is hospitality ​— the ‌craft ​of receiving ​greatness and ​giving it ‌words. ​The god ‌whose name ​means ‌'foremost' is ​the one ‌who stands ‌where ​the living ​greet the ​dead ​and finds ‌the sentence ‌both can ​bear.[^1]
